Chapter Two: Navigating Identity and Belonging
As time goes by, the question of identity really starts to take center stage for those who’ve been adopted. It’s a journey—sometimes private, sometimes played out in the open—where figuring out who you are isn’t always so simple. That feeling of being just a little bit different? It might be quiet, or sometimes it hits hard, but either way, it really shapes how adoptees see themselves and the world around them.
Imagine a young adult, growing up in a home filled with love. Family gatherings are bright, full of laughter, warm hugs, inside jokes. But every now and then, something feels just a bit off—maybe it’s a certain smile, a craving for foods no one else at the table recognizes, or a skin tone that stands out in family photos. These differences aren’t usually talked about, but they’re always there, quietly shaping that person’s sense of self.
School can bring its own challenges. Classmates might ask, “Why don’t you look like your parents?” or “Where are you really from?” They might not mean any harm, but those questions can sting. Suddenly, you’re forced to think about things you might not have answers for. Over time, the urge to understand your beginnings gets stronger. Some adoptees find comfort in the stories their adoptive parents share, while others feel a deep curiosity about the families they’ve never known.
Let’s look at one woman’s story. She was adopted from another country as a baby, growing up as the only person of her background in her entire community. As she got older, she felt the weight of that cultural gap. The food, the holidays, the traditions from her birth country—they were all unfamiliar, and she found herself struggling to bring these two parts of her identity together. Eventually, she decided to return to her birth country, hoping to find answers. That trip was both thrilling and tough. She met people who looked just like her, heard her birth language spoken for the very first time, and even visited the orphanage where her life began. It didn’t solve everything, but it helped her feel a little more whole.
It’s not just adoptees who face these questions. Adoptive parents feel them too. Many wonder, “How do I help my child feel comfortable in their own skin?” Take one father, for instance—he noticed his son felt out of place as the only child of color in their neighborhood. So, he made a point of finding families with similar backgrounds. They went to cultural festivals, tried out new recipes together, and filled their home with books and movies that reflected his son’s heritage. Did it erase every challenge? No. But it showed, in a powerful way, that every part of his son’s identity truly mattered.
Building a sense of belonging isn’t a one-time thing. For some, it’s about searching for birth relatives, piecing together family history, or learning about cultural traditions. For others, it’s about connecting with other adoptees, sharing stories and experiences that people outside adoption just might not understand. The path can be messy—there are moments of frustration, self-doubt, and sometimes even anger. But with time, many adoptees start to see their unique backgrounds as a real source of strength.
A lot of people think adoption wipes the slate clean, but the truth is, it’s much more complex than that. These stories show us that identity is shaped by both where we come from and where we’re headed—by the families we’re born into, and the ones we choose. Belonging isn’t about picking one side or the other. It’s about weaving all those different pieces together into something new, and uniquely your own.
